The wind on the Isle of Skerry didn’t just blow; it screamed. It tore at the stone walls of the lighthouse, a constant, rhythmic assault that Elias had endured for thirty years. He was old now, his joints stiff as rusted hinges, and his eyes, once sharp enough to spot a gull from a mile out, were clouded by cataracts. The light above him still turned, a mechanical heartbeat in the dark, but Elias felt he was fading into the same obscurity as the rocks below.

On a Tuesday, when the storm was at its peak, the mail boat arrived. It was an anomaly. The sea was too rough for the small skiff to navigate the channel safely. Yet there it was, bobbing violently against the jetty, carrying a single, wax-sealed envelope. The postman, a young man with rain-soaked hair, handed it over without a word, his face pale with fear or exhaustion, before retreating into the churning waves.

Elias took the letter inside, shaking water from his coat. The paper was thick, cream-colored, and smelled faintly of ozone and lavender—a scent that did not belong to this damp, salt-heavy world. The seal bore no crest, only a symbol: a circle bisected by a vertical line, resembling a keyhole.

He broke the seal. The handwriting inside was elegant, looping, and utterly unfamiliar.

*Dear Keeper,*

*You are wondering how I know your name. You are wondering if this is a trick of the mind, brought on by isolation and age. It is neither. My name is Elara. I am your great-granddaughter. I write to you from 2147.*

Elias’s hands trembled. He looked around the empty room, the shadows dancing wildly in the flickering lantern light.

*We have lost the coast,* the letter continued. *The storms you endure now are merely the prologue. In my time, the sea has swallowed the mainland. We live in the high places, in the spires that remain. But we remember the light. Not just the beam, but the promise of it. The idea that someone stands watch, that darkness is not absolute.*
